Q: How to place red color asterisk mark after text in placeholder using jQuery? A:

Hey so sadly you cant have two different colors in a placeholder text. Thats just not how placeholders work - they only allow one color.

But dont worry theres a workaround! You can fake it by putting the red asterisk outside the input using CSS. Heres how:

Just add a span after your input with the asterisk and position it so it looks like its inside. You can use CSS like position absolute to put it right where you want it.

Or you can put a label before the input that says the field name with a red asterisk and leave the placeholder for something else.

Basically placeholders are just plain text so you cant style parts of them differently. Hope that makes sense!

Q: How can I set up a new comment string in PyCharm for fragment of DTL code in .html file? A:

The next solution is work well only for one separate string of code. And does not work with block of code.

We have to write a macro and then assing a combination of keys for it:

Start macro recording

Edit > Macros > Start Macro Recording

Press Home to put cursor at the beginning of the string

Then type {#

Press End to put cursor at the end of the string

Type #}

Stop macro recording:

Edit > Macros > Stop Macro Recording

Confirm the code of macro

Edit > Macros > Edit Macros

Name it e.g., DTL_comment

Then assign key coombination

Ctrl+Alt+S > Keymap > Macros > Invoke Macro >Right Click > Add Keyboard Shortcut > Ctr+Shift+Q

Press Apply, OK

So, put cursor on the string you want to comment with {# and #}

and then press Ctr+Shift+Q.

Q: Splitting C code into separate files without using functions A:

I want to split blocks of code from the main main.c ... but I don't want to use functions

I'm sorry to tell you this, but - you should change what you want; it is based on false assumptions:

I don’t want to use functions because that introduces additional overhead (function call, stack usage, etc.).

Actually,

  • The use of functions does not necessarily introduce additional overhead. In fact, if you a function in the same translation unit (i.e. source file+headers) - called just once - the compiler is likely to just inline it, if any optimization is enabled - and you've marked the function as static, so the compiler knows the function won't be used elsewhere. If a function is inlined, no call will be made nor anything pushed onto the stack.

  • The extent of the overhead of calling a handful of functions once, on a modern CPU, is several nanoseconds. This is entirely inconsequential for your program, as opposed to any number of other aspects of it.

Such premature design choices in the name of optimization of universally seen as undesirable, with Donald Knuth known to have been said that "premature optimization is the root of all evil". Naturally that is a bit harsh for a small C program, but you may want to read this article/blog post:

Why Premature Optimization is the Root of All Evil?

  • Finally, Performance improvement is not the only aspect of software you should consider. There are many important considerations than saving time on making function calls: Readability; maintainability; testability separation of concerns; locality of definitions; and others - all in favor of breaking down your work into smaller functions rather than writing one big sequence of instructions for everything.
